title: Matthew 15:1–9
context: Pharisees and scribes arrive from Jerusalem and accuse Jesus’ disciples of breaking the tradition of the elders by eating with unwashed hands. Jesus turns the charge: their Corban practice voids God’s command to honor father and mother, and Isaiah’s word exposes lip-service worship that teaches human commandments as doctrine.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 15:1–9, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The elders - The chief doctors or, teachers among the Jews. They wash not their hands when they eat bread - Food in general is termed bread in Hebrew; so that to eat bread is the same as to make a meal. honour thy father and mother - Which implies all such relief as they stand in need of.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 15:1–9)

reformed.quote: As the fault that is here corrected is not only common but highly dangerous, the passage is particularly worthy of our attention. We see the extraordinary insolence that is displayed by men as to the form and manner of worshipping God; for they are perpetually contriving new modes of worship, and when any one wishes to be thought wiser than others, he displays his ingenuity on this subject.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 15:1–9)

verses.text: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Leaders travel from the holy city to confront Jesus. Official religion arrives with a question already loaded against Him and His disciples.

This is a test of hearts. Grace has brought truth near Jerusalem’s teachers; they remain responsible for how they receive or resist the One standing before them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew’s “from Jerusalem” marks weighty opposition. The center of Israel’s religious authority opens a conflict that will run toward the cross.

This meeting is not random friction. The Father’s purpose includes exposing tradition that smothers His word, even when the challenge comes from the capital.

verses.text: “Why do your disciples disobey the tradition of the elders? For they don’t wash their hands when they eat bread.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The charge is tradition, not Moses: unwashed hands at meals. Human custom is treated as if it were God’s fence around purity.

Religious habits can feel holy while sidelining God’s actual commands. Hearers are called to weigh tradition by Scripture, not to baptize every elder custom as binding.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Tradition of the elders” is named as the standard. Ritual handwashing becomes the measure of faithfulness in their mouths.

When man-made fences become law, the conscience is captured. Christ will reclaim the Word’s supremacy over inherited rules that pose as piety.

verses.text: He answered them, “Why do you also disobey the commandment of God because of your tradition?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus answers charge with charge: they break God’s commandment for tradition’s sake. The question is not anti-tradition in the abstract; it is anti-substituting custom for obedience.

Arminians stress a sincere summons back to God’s revealed will. Grace exposes the swap so hearers can repent of elevating human rules over divine command.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ’s counter-question unveils the breach. Tradition is not neutral here; it is the tool by which God’s commandment is broken.

The Son judges religion by the Word. Where custom cancels command, He names the guilt and will not flatter the system.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject tradition that overrides God’s command. Arminians stress a grace-enabled call to repent of that swap and obey Scripture; Reformed commentators often emphasize Christ’s authoritative exposure of a system already voiding the Word under God’s judicial purpose.

verses.text: For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus cites God’s own voice: honor father and mother, and the severe word against reviling parents. Fifth-commandment love is not optional piety.

Grace restores weight to family honor. Disciples are responsible to keep God’s commands in ordinary relationships, not only in ritual correctness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two texts from the Law ground the rebuke. God commanded; the issue is divine authority, not rabbinic preference.

The Law still reveals God’s holy will. Christ upholds the commandment even as He will fulfill all righteousness for His people.

verses.text: But you say, ‘Whoever may tell his father or his mother, “Whatever help you might otherwise have gotten from me is a gift devoted to God,”
verses.arminianNotes:
“But you say” introduces a religious loophole: dedicating support “to God” so parents are denied. Sacred language covers neglect.

Arminians name this as accountable hypocrisy. Grace does not bless vows that starve parents while sounding devout. Love of God never cancels love of neighbor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Human speech (“you say”) stands against God’s command. Corban-style dedication becomes a pious excuse to withhold honor.

False worship invents escapes from duty. Christ exposes how religion can be weaponized against the very people the Law protects.

verses.text: he shall not honor his father or mother.’ You have made the commandment of God void because of your tradition.
verses.arminianNotes:
The punch line: tradition makes void the word of God. What God spoke is emptied so custom can stand.

This is resistible light refused. Hearers who cling to loopholes remain responsible for silencing Scripture in practice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Made void is judicial clarity. Tradition is not merely mistaken; it nullifies God’s word for the sake of the system.

Christ guards the Word’s integrity. Where human religion cancels divine speech, the Messiah names the void and will plant what the Father plants.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that tradition can nullify Scripture. Arminians typically stress moral responsibility to stop voiding God’s word and return to obedience; Calvinists stress Christ’s verdict that such religion already stands condemned as making void what God has spoken.

verses.text: You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hypocrites” is not a slur for disagreement; it names a split between claim and heart. Isaiah already mapped this people.

Arminian readers hear a warning meant to wake. Prophetic words still call for repentance; grace invites a return from play-acting worship to true fear of God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus ties His hearers to Isaiah’s oracle. The prophet’s “you” lands on this generation’s leaders.

Scripture interprets Scripture, and Christ applies it with authority. Hypocrisy is unmasked by the Word that searches hearts.

verses.text: ‘These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lips near, heart far: worship can be verbally correct and relationally empty. God wants the heart, not flattery.

Assisting grace softens hearts to draw near in truth. Hearers remain called to close the gap between speech and love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Isaiah’s diagnosis is heart-distance under lip-honor. External religion without inward nearness is vanity before God.

Comfort: only God can bring far hearts near. The same Lord who exposes distance will create true worshipers by His Spirit.
verses.keyContrast: Both insist God requires the heart, not mere words. Arminians typically highlight a grace-enabled turning of the heart toward God; Reformed Christians highlight that nearness of heart is God’s regenerating gift, not the fruit of unaided resolve.

verses.text: And they worship me in vain, teaching as doctrine rules made by men.’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Vain worship teaches human commandments as if they were divine doctrines. The classroom of tradition displaces God’s curriculum.

Arminian interpreters urge reformation of teaching: measure every must by Scripture. Grace enables teachers and hearers to refuse man-made burdens posed as gospel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Worship is “in vain” when men’s commands are taught as doctrine. The issue is authority: whose word binds the conscience?

Christ restores the Word to the center. Empty worship is judged so that true fear of God may rise where His commandments alone rule as doctrine.
